summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been legal in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate-motivated conduct on the basis of sexual orientation is criminalised across several statutes. Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence on that ground.

Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 inserted sexual orientation into Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (five years).

A Monegasque court applied this framework in July 2010, sentencing a man to five days' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. It is the only documented prosecution in the sources.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned by law; Outright International reports such discrimination as rare but describes protections as very limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, a cohabitation agreement signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry.

Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco. LGBTIQ visibility is limited: roughly ten people are reported to dare to be openly out, no gay Pride is held anywhere in the principality, and there are no official gay bars, clubs or events. Visitors are directed to France or Italy for Pride.

Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it maintains close cultural and economic ties with France. France handles defence, and its armed forces allow openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve; Monaco itself maintains only a National Guard.
tangentialFactors:
Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings. ILGA-Europe's 2019 assessment placed the principality 45th of 49 European countries. Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo summarised the position as "C'est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Same-sex partners have no access to equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax purposes rather than like married couples, and the cohabitation agreement is equally open to siblings and to parents and children.

A 2011 anti-discrimination bill would have required an annual school programme across primary and secondary cycles to sensitise pupils against racism and all discrimination covered by its article 1, including sexual orientation. The Council of Government did not approve the bill, and its replacement of 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

The 2023 US State Department Human Rights Report recorded no significant changes for Monaco and limited its significant issues to libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced; no torture, arbitrary detention or similar abuses were reported.

Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which treats homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. The gay travel guide Gay Voyageur pitches the roughly 200-hectare state as a luxury and relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene, and points visitors to Marseille, Nice and Lyon for gay nightlife and events.
localsOnly:
The contrat de vie commune entered Parliament on 16 April 2018, was approved unanimously by the National Council on 4 December 2019, and took effect six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco, on 27 June 2020. The agreement is executed before a notary and lodged with a public registry.

Residents have no statutory route to change legal gender, and no anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, education or services. Reported discrimination is described as rare, but there is no complaint mechanism to test that.

The 2012 replacement anti-discrimination bill left residents without the school sensitisation programme contemplated in 2011. Employment and public-accommodation protection on sexual-orientation grounds remains unenacted.

Monaco's only military formation is the National Guard; defence rests with France, whose forces accept openly LGBT service members.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports a prosecution under Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 or under Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019, so enforcement of those provisions beyond the July 2010 case is unresolved.

No source addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice, customs questioning, or the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports at Monegasque borders. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether a visitor's documents are inspected for sex or gender inconsistencies.

Facilities, healthcare access, and any rule on restroom or single-sex-space use for transgender visitors are not sourced here. Neither are hate-crime statistics, police reporting practices, or the operation of the protection machinery for LGBTIQ visitors.

Outright International's characterisation of discrimination as rare is self-reported and carries no underlying data in the inventory; the absence of a statutory ban means official statistics on complaints cannot exist.

The July 2010 judgment is described only in secondary coverage; the court, the exact provision applied and any appeal outcome are not available from these sources.
